The verse carries a deeply practical spiritual message — that believers need not despair when they see falsehood gaining momentum, for Allah's counter-plan is always at work, always ahead, and always superior. It instills trust in divine wisdom and patience in the face of opposition.
16.layer2: The term 'kayd' (كيد) in verse 16 is a verbal noun derived from the root k-y-d, denoting a concealed and methodical plan, often with connotations of a trap or stratagem executed covertly. Classical grammarians note that 'kaydan' functions here as a maf'ul mutlaq — an absolute object — reinforcing the verb 'akidu,' intensifying the declaration: 'I am indeed planning a most thorough plan.' Imam al-Tabari in his Jami al-Bayan notes that this verse establishes a direct divine parallel to the human scheming described in verse 15. The disbelievers plot, but Allah's plan encompasses and overrides theirs entirely. Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim explains that Allah's 'kayd' here refers to the divine stratagem of granting apparent respite to the disbelievers — allowing them to persist in their plotting — while simultaneously preparing the conditions for their destruction and the ultimate triumph of the believers. This mirrors the Quranic theme found in Surah Al-Imran (3:54): 'They planned and Allah planned, and Allah is the best of planners.' Ibn Kathir also links verse 16 contextually to 31:24, where Allah says He lets the disbelievers enjoy a little while before bringing them into a grievous punishment. Al-Qurtubi in his Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran emphasizes that using the word 'kayd' for Allah — a term associated with concealment — conveys that Allah's plan unfolds in ways unseen by the plotters themselves until the moment it is enacted. There are no fiqh rulings directly derived from this verse, but it carries significant theological weight regarding the certainty of divine justice and the futility of opposing Allah's decree.
16.layer3: From the perspective of usul al-tafsir, verse 16 presents an important instance of what scholars classify as tashbih al-fi'l — the attribution of an action to Allah using a term ordinarily associated with human conduct, in this case 'kayd' (plotting or stratagem). The Ash'ari and Maturidi schools of kalam approach such attributions via the principle of tanzih: the action is real and affirmative but free from any anthropomorphic implication. Allah's 'kayd' is not reactive human scheming; it is the unfolding of divine qadar with absolute authority and wisdom. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb discusses the rhetorical dimension of this verse, noting that by mirroring the language used for the disbelievers' plotting in verse 15 ('innahum yakiduna kaydan'), Allah employs a form of istidraj — He lets opponents believe they are succeeding precisely as His own plan is being executed. Al-Razi also highlights that the divine 'kayd' in this verse should be understood in light of its outcomes — the complete historical collapse of Mecca's opposition to Islam — making it a prospective reference to events that were then future but are now historical. From the perspective of 'ilm al-munasabat (the science of Quranic coherence), this verse serves as the pivot of the surah's closing argument: the cosmic proofs of Allah's power in verses 1-14 lead to the affirmation in verses 15-17 that this same power will be directed against those who deny the Quran. Ibn Ashur in al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir notes the surah's concluding verses form a tight chiastic structure in which divine omnipotence frames the narrative of human arrogance and its inevitable defeat.

concepts.title: Grant Respite
concepts.coreInsight: Famahhil al-kafirina - so grant respite to the disbelievers. Allah commands patience rather than immediate punishment, giving them time to reflect and potentially repent.
concepts.whyItMatters: This teaches believers to be patient with opposition rather than seeking immediate revenge. Allah's timing is perfect - He gives people opportunities to change before consequences arrive.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: فمہل الکافرین - تو کافروں کو مہلت دو۔ اللہ فوری سزا کی بجائے صبر کا حکم دیتا ہے، انہیں غور کرنے اور ممکنہ طور پر توبہ کرنے کا وقت دیتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یہ مومنین کو سکھاتا ہے کہ فوری بدلہ لینے کی بجائے مخالفت کے ساتھ صبر کریں۔ اللہ کا وقت کامل ہے - وہ لوگوں کو نتائج آنے سے پہلے تبدیل ہونے کے مواقع دیتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: فمهل الكافرين - فأمهل الكافرين. يأمر الله بالصبر بدلاً من العقاب الفوري، مما يمنحهم وقتاً للتفكير والتوبة المحتملة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: يعلم هذا المؤمنين أن يكونوا صبورين مع المعارضة بدلاً من السعي للانتقام الفوري. توقيت الله مثالي - إنه يمنح الناس فرصاً للتغيير قبل وصول العواقب.

concepts.title: Leave Them Awhile
concepts.coreInsight: Amhilhum ruwaydan - leave them for a little while. The diminutive form 'ruwaydan' (a little while) indicates that their respite is temporary, not permanent.
concepts.whyItMatters: Divine justice is delayed but never denied. Wrongdoers get time to repent, but if they persist, consequences will inevitably follow. Patience doesn't mean acceptance of oppression.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: امہلہم رویدا - انہیں تھوڑی دیر کے لیے چھوڑ دو۔ تصغیری صیغہ 'رویدا' (تھوڑی دیر) اس بات کی نشاندہی کرتا ہے کہ ان کی مہلت عارضی ہے، مستقل نہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: الہی انصاف میں تاخیر ہوتی ہے لیکن کبھی انکار نہیں ہوتا۔ ظالموں کو توبہ کرنے کا وقت ملتا ہے، لیکن اگر وہ جاری رہیں، تو نتائج لازمی طور پر آئیں گے۔ صبر کا مطلب ظلم کی قبولیت نہیں ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: أمهلهم رويداً - اتركهم قليلاً. الصيغة التصغيرية 'رويداً' (قليلاً) تشير إلى أن إمهالهم مؤقت وليس دائماً.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: العدل الإلهي يتأخر لكنه لا يُنكر أبداً. يحصل الظالمون على وقت للتوبة، لكن إذا استمروا، فستتبع العواقب حتماً. الصبر لا يعني قبول الظلم.

concepts.title: Divine Forbearance
concepts.coreInsight: This command shows Allah's hilm (forbearance) - He delays punishment despite having absolute power, giving wrongdoers chances to reform before facing justice.
concepts.whyItMatters: We should emulate Allah's forbearance in dealing with those who wrong us. Quick anger isn't strength - patience with wisdom is the divine attribute we should adopt.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: یہ حکم اللہ کی حلم (بردباری) کو ظاہر کرتا ہے - وہ مطلق طاقت رکھنے کے باوجود سزا میں تاخیر کرتا ہے، ظالموں کو انصاف کا سامنا کرنے سے پہلے اصلاح کے مواقع دیتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: ہمیں ان لوگوں کے ساتھ معاملہ کرتے وقت اللہ کی بردباری کی تقلید کرنی چاہیے جو ہمارے ساتھ زیادتی کرتے ہیں۔ فوری غصہ طاقت نہیں ہے - حکمت کے ساتھ صبر وہ الہی صفت ہے جو ہمیں اپنانی چاہیے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يظهر هذا الأمر حلم الله - إنه يؤخر العقاب رغم امتلاكه القوة المطلقة، مما يمنح الظالمين فرصاً للإصلاح قبل مواجهة العدالة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: يجب أن نقلد حلم الله في التعامل مع من يظلموننا. الغضب السريع ليس قوة - الصبر بحكمة هو الصفة الإلهية التي يجب أن نتبناها.

17.layer4: Examining both Shia and Sunni interpretations of this verse reveals harmonious understanding of its essential message while showing different emphases in application. Classical Sunni commentators like Ibn Kathir explain that this command to grant respite demonstrates Allah's mercy and the Prophet's noble character, allowing opponents time that some might use for repentance. Al-Tabari's comprehensive tafsir notes that several Quraysh leaders who initially persecuted Islam, including figures like Khalid ibn al-Walid, eventually embraced faith partly because they were given time to observe and reflect. This aligns with Shia interpretations though Shia scholars additionally emphasize how the Ahlul Bayt implemented this principle throughout their lives despite facing persecution, particularly Imam Ali's patient restraint during the early caliphate period and Imam Husayn's patient negotiation before Karbala. Both traditions agree that this verse establishes a fundamental Islamic ethical principle, that certainty in truth allows believers to respond to opposition with patience rather than aggression. Modern Sunni and Shia scholars both cite this verse when discussing appropriate Muslim responses to contemporary challenges, emphasizing that patient adherence to Islamic principles while trusting divine justice represents the prophetic model. Where interpretive traditions enrich each other is in historical examples, with Sunni scholarship emphasizing the eventual conversion of former enemies, while Shia scholarship emphasizes maintaining truth with patience even when opponents never change, as both outcomes serve divine wisdom.

17.layer4_ar: يكشف تأمل التفسيرين الشيعي والسني لهذه الآية عن توافق جوهري في الجوهر مع تمايز في التأكيدات عند التطبيق. فالمفسرون الكلاسيكيون السنة كابن كثير يُوضِّحون أن هذا الأمر بالإمهال يُجلِّي رحمة الله وكريم خلق النبي مانحاً الخصومَ وقتاً ربما يستثمره بعضهم للتوبة. وتفسير الطبري الموسوعي يُلاحظ أن بعض قادة قريش ممن أسرفوا في اضطهاد الإسلام، في مقدمتهم خالد بن الوليد، أسلموا في نهاية المطاف جزئياً لأنهم أُمهلوا ليشاهدوا ويتفكروا. وهذا يتسق مع التفسيرات الشيعية وإن أضاف العلماء الشيعة أن أهل البيت طبَّقوا هذا المبدأ طوال حياتهم رغم معاناتهم من الاضطهاد، ولا سيما صبر الإمام علي في صدر الخلافة، وصبر الإمام الحسين والتفاوض في ما قبل كربلاء. ويتفق التراثان على أن هذه الآية تُؤسِّس مبدأً أخلاقياً إسلامياً جوهرياً: اليقين بصدق الحق يُمكِّن المؤمنين من مواجهة المعارضة بالصبر لا بالعدوانية. ويستشهد علماء الشيعة والسنة المعاصرون بهذه الآية في مناقشة استجابة المسلمين للتحديات المعاصرة مُشدِّدين على أن التمسك بالمبادئ الإسلامية بصبر مع الثقة بالعدل الإلهي هو النموذج النبوي الأصيل. والتراثان يُثريان بعضهما في الاستشهاد التاريخي: يُبرز المنهج السني إسلام الأعداء السابقين مثالاً، بينما يُشدِّد المنهج الشيعي على الثبات على الحق بصبر حتى حين لا يتحول الخصم، إذ كلا الحالين يخدمان الحكمة الإلهية.
17.layer1: The final verse of Surah At-Tariq — 'So grant respite to the disbelievers; give them a little time' — is both a command to the Prophet and a closing statement of divine confidence. The Arabic reads: 'fa-mahhil al-kafirin amhilhum ruwaydan.' Allah instructs the Prophet not to be anxious or hurried in seeking the punishment of those who oppose the truth. The word 'ruwaydan' is particularly expressive — it is the diminutive form of the Arabic word for 'respite,' meaning 'just a little while,' 'a brief delay,' conveying the idea that the time given to the disbelievers is vanishingly short in the grand scale of divine justice. This verse closes the surah with a note of absolute calm and certainty. The tone is not one of weakness or hesitation — it is the composure of one who knows the outcome is already decided. Classical scholars explain that the command 'give them respite' was initially a directive for patience before the battles of early Islam, and some scholars such as Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari note that this instruction was later superseded — in terms of its passive application — by the verses of jihad. However, its spiritual message remains eternally relevant: Allah's justice is not delayed but measured, not absent but patient. The verse encourages the believer to trust in Allah's timing and not to feel that the temporary comfort of the disbelievers constitutes any victory for them. In reality, it is the giving of rope — and the end has already been written by the One who declared in the previous verse, 'And I am planning a plan.'
17.layer2: The grammatical construction of verse 17 is noteworthy for its rhetorical doubling. The command begins with 'fa-mahhil' — from the verb mahhala, meaning to grant time gradually and slowly — and is immediately followed by 'amhilhum' from the related root amhala, meaning to give respite or delay. Scholars of Arabic rhetoric note that this doubling (known as 'al-ta'kid bil-muradif') serves to intensify and affirm the command, leaving no ambiguity: the Prophet is being told emphatically and with all clarity to hold back, be patient, and allow the divine plan to unfold. The word 'ruwaydan' functions as a hal (circumstantial qualifier) or as a maf'ul mutlaq and is the tasghir (diminutive form) of 'rawd' or 'irwad,' stressing the brevity of the respite — it is short, measurable, and fixed in Allah's knowledge. Al-Tabari in Jami al-Bayan reports that many companions of the Prophet understood this verse as a declaration that the disbelievers' enjoyment was already near its end, and that the verse was revealed to comfort the Prophet and steel the believers' resolve during the difficult Meccan period. Ibn Kathir connects this verse to Quran 31:24 — 'We let them enjoy for a little while, then We shall oblige them to enter a severe punishment' — drawing a clear thematic parallel. Some scholars including al-Qurtubi noted the question of naskh (abrogation): whether this verse's implicit instruction of patience was abrogated by the verse of the sword (9:5), though the majority position holds that the spiritual meaning of divine patience and measured timing remains permanently valid.
17.layer3: Verse 17 occupies a critical position in the science of al-fawasil — the study of Quranic verse endings — as it closes the surah with 'ruwaydan,' a word whose soft phonetic quality (the diminutive ending in '-an') contrasts powerfully with the gravity of its meaning. This literary tension between gentle sound and weighty content is a hallmark of Makkan surahs, and Ibn Ashur in al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir identifies this as a deliberate stylistic choice that leaves the listener in a state of contemplative awe rather than rhetorical agitation. The question of naskh in this verse has been treated carefully by usuliyyun. Al-Qurtubi references the opinion that the command to grant respite was abrogated by Quran 9:5 and the subsequent directives for active confrontation with polytheism. However, scholars of the Hanafi school, as recorded in their usul works, distinguish between the temporal application of such a command (which may have shifted) and its theological content (which is eternal), preserving the verse's relevance as a statement of divine sovereignty over time and outcomes. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb treats 'ruwaydan' as an expression of divine irony — the 'little while' afforded to the disbelievers is framed from Allah's eternal perspective, making even decades or centuries a brief, inconsequential interval. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran describes the closing of the surah as an act of supreme composure on the part of the divine address — not a threat shouted in anger, but a calm decree issued from a position of total and unchallenged power, leaving the disbelievers with nothing but the certainty of an approaching, inevitable reckoning.
